title: How Do You Know When To Keep Developing Someone And When To Stop
author: Summer Mulder
summary: Mulder offers a framework for the difficult leadership decision of whether to continue developing an underperforming team member or make a change. Drawing on EOS's Right Person/Right Seat assessment, she argues that many underperformance issues stem from clarity deficits or role misalignment rather than capability gaps. She identifies the two common errors: giving up too soon before systems are in place, and holding on too long out of loyalty or discomfort, which damages team culture by signaling unequal standards. Her decision framework rests on five diagnostic questions: Has clarity been provided? Do they understand the job's outcomes? Are they respected by peers and reports? Is there genuine desire to grow? And crucially, is the leader complicit in the underperformance? A written scorecard makes these decisions less about personal feelings and more about data, though honest interpretation remains essential. The answer is not a fixed timeline but rather long enough to set someone up to win, short enough to avoid organizational drag.
points: Right Person/Right Seat framework from EOS distinguishes cultural fit from role fit, with misalignment on either dimension requiring different responses.
Unclear roles and undefined standards generate underperformance that masquerades as a people problem; a written scorecard transforms subjective decisions into data-driven clarity.
Delayed people decisions damage team culture by signaling unequal standards to high performers, making non-action more costly than decisive action.
The four diagnostic questions (clarity, job understanding, respect, desire) plus honest self-assessment about leader complicity create a framework for development vs. exit decisions.
Development windows vary by person and season; the art of leadership is giving enough time to set someone up for success without indefinitely carrying non-performers.
quotes: When you keep someone who isn't performing and everyone around them knows it, you are not being kind. You are being complicit. You are sending a message to every high performer on that team that the standard doesn't actually apply equally.
A lot of underperformance that looks like a people problem is actually a clarity problem. The person didn't fail. The system failed to give them what they needed to succeed.

You can have a Right Person in the Wrong Seat. Someone who is a cultural fit but isn't performing because the role doesn't match their strengths. The answer there is usually a conversation about repositioning, not an exit.

A scorecard makes a lot of this cleaner. When the outcomes are written down and the standard is clear and the timeline is agreed upon, the decision becomes less about how you feel about someone and more about what the data actually says.

The answer to how long do you give someone is: long enough to set them up to succeed, short enough that you're not letting the organization carry someone who can't or won't grow into what's needed. That window is different for every person, every role, every season of the business.
The most expensive people decisions I've ever seen weren't the ones that got made. They were the ones that didn't.” Archived from Summer Mulder Substack on May 3, 2026 by Tim.
